#1039. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

England want to host the Nations League, but things are never easy hosting international football in this country

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Football Association has registered interest in England hosting the Nations League finals.

On Sunday, the Three Lions booked their place as one of the top seeds in the newly expanded quarter-finals of the competition, beating world champions Spain to set up a clash against a second seed in March.

And England could well be playing a semi on home soil, if the FA has anything to do with it.

According to Sami Mokbel of the BBC, England, Spain and France have all contacted UEFA, expressing their desire to host the final four games of next summer's Nations League competition.

The competition began in 2019, with the inaugural finals both hosted and ultimately won by Portugal, before heading to Italy (2021), the Netherlands (2023), and, most recently, Germany (2025).

England will face one of Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in the last eight of the competition – and could well become the first host of the finals not to reach the final four, given the new format of the competition.

So far, the only publically announced events at Wembley this June are two concerts from Newcastle United fan, Sam Fender, though these are scheduled to take place after the Nations League is due to be played.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the FA would welcome the opportunity to host a mini-tournament with the European Championship coming to the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland in 2028 – with other venues in consideration for hosting duties next summer.

While the Etihad Stadium is booked for much of June for Oasis's Live '27 tour, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium is, so far, free to host, with cult noughties emo band Fall Out Boy and stadium rock veterans U2 booked either side of when the semi-finals would take place.

The Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, meanwhile, could well host its first major internationals.

This isn't a new conundrum for the FA to solve, with the Community Shield recently affected by Wembley's commitments beyond football.

This summer, the season's curtain-raiser was held in Cardiff at the Millennium Stadium, while 2022 saw Erling Haaland make his Manchester City debut at the King Power Stadium in the fixture.

England will play home and away in the next international break in the Nations League quarter.

James Anderson’s franchise cricket return ended in defeat as Napoli Knights lost to Rome Gladiators by six wickets in their Italia T10 league opener.

Anderson is co-owner of Napoli Knights, with the 44-year-old's appearance his first since being released by boyhood club Lancashire at the end of the season.

Napoli Knights are one of six teams in the nine-day tournament at Roma Cricket Ground, running until November 28, with Anderson's side restricted to 73-9 after losing the toss and batting first.

Anderson finished nought not out from one delivery faced, scampering a bye from the final ball of the innings, before taking 0-14 from two overs during Rome Gladiators' successful chase.

England's history-making Test bowler conceded just three from a tight opening over of Rome's chase, before being hit down the ground by Singh for a maximum - during an 11-run over - when returning for a second stint later in the innings.

Anthony Mosca fired an unbeaten 45 from 27 deliveries and Jaspreet Singh ended 15 not out from nine, as Rome Gladiators claimed a five-wicket win with two balls remaining.

Wayne Madsen, captaining the Napoli Knights: "It's fantastic to have Jimmy [Anderson] here. He's inspirational to so many of us.

"To be playing with him, and for him to share his knowledge with this group, is amazing. I think, as we've seen, he has still got the skill to go out there and perform at the top level."

Napoli Knights have further matches against Brescia Lions (Saturday), Venice Livewire (Sunday), Milan Icons (Monday) and Bologna Hurricanes (TBC).

Anderson has joined Surrey ahead of the 2027 season in the Rothesay County Championship, having been left "sad" and "quite shocked" by his contract not being extended by Lancashire.

"I also think that I can bring a lot to the team off the field and help those young players who are looking to develop their skillset and go on and represent their country."

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Bukayo Saka faces a longer spell on the sidelines but there was positive news for long-term absentee William Saliba

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal winger Bukayo Saka is facing another month on the sidelines as he continues to recover from a thigh injury, taking his absence to eight weeks.

Saka picked up the injury early in a Champions League game against Bayern Munich on 21 October.

Manager Mikel Arteta issued the update at a press conference ahead of the Premier League’s return, with Arsenal heading to Newcastle for their first game since the international break.

Arteta said Saka had undergone more tests on the issue and was “evolving really well”.

He said: “It looks like it’s going to be an eight-week injury, more or less, so I think it’s four at the moment. Still a while before he's back with the team.”

Arsenal will also be missing midfielder Martin Zubimendi for a “few weeks” after he picked up a hamstring injury with Spain during the Nations League break, but the Gunners were handed a boost with centre-back William Saliba finally available for selection after a lengthy absence.

The Frenchman has been struggling with a back injury which he was managing at the end of the 2025-26 campaign, and it brought his World Cup to a premature end as he was forced off half an hour into France’s semi-final defeat.

But he did not require surgery and after several months out, has now played two practice matches and is set to be included in the squad.

Arteta said: “He's ready. He's in a good condition. He played two games, one behind closed doors and one more official and he did really well and he's in good condition.

On Zubimendi, Arteta said: “He's out. Unfortunately he has a slight problem in his hamstring. He wasn't too concerned after the game but after the MRI scan showed there's an injury there and he's going to be out for a few weeks.”

Arteta also responded to the idea that Fantasy Premier League (FPL) selections by top-flight players, staff and family members have contributed towards team news leaks in recent weeks.

He said: “It's a topic. This is the kind of things that are happening in our society right now and it's something new, we haven't dealt with it and we have to put new things in place.

“The confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and what you're trying to do and that should be kept as a huge secret. And we will take measures to make sure that doesn't happen.”

#1033. University students are biggest spreaders of COVID

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a big part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

The study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest among adolescents aged 15 to 18 in schools, undergraduates at university, and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

The analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences with medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” says Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts, between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage says. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.

England face a rematch of their World Cup quarter-final against Norway, while Spain play France in a blockbuster quarter-final

England will play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in March, in a rematch of their World Cup quarter-final.

Jude Bellingham scored twice in Miami as England came from behind to end Norway’s sensational World Cup run back in July.

But Erling Haaland’s team will be out for revenge after their incredible comeback to beat Denmark secured progress to the two-legged Nations League quarter-finals.

The Three Lions, who topped Group A3 with a 3-2 win over world champions Spain, will travel to Oslo in the first leg before hosting the second leg as they bid to reach the Nations League Finals in June.

Follow latest updates from the quarter-final draw below:

England will play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in March, in a rematch of their World Cup quarter-final.

Jude Bellingham scored twice in Miami as England came from behind to end Norway’s sensational World Cup run back in July.

But Erling Haaland’s team will be out for revenge after their incredible comeback to beat Denmark secured progress to the two-legged Nations League quarter-finals.

The Three Lions, who topped Group A3 with a 3-2 win over world champions Spain, will travel to Oslo in the first leg before hosting the second leg as they bid to reach the Nations League Finals in June.

Should England progress to the semi-finals, they will play either Jurgen Klopp’s Germany or Belgium, while the other semi-final will see either Spain or France play against Portugal or the Netherlands.

In the Nations League play-offs, which were also decided during the draw in Nyon, Wales will play Slovenia as they bid to retain their top-tier status.

The Republic of Ireland face a tough test against Croatia as they attempt to reach League A for the first time. Both ties will be played across two legs, also in March.

Norway will be out for revenge against England, who could face Jurgen Klopp’s Germany if they reach the semi-finals.

England have been handed a suspended ban for away supporters as a result of “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” by fans during Sunday’s 3-2 win over Spain in Madrid.

The ban, which would apply to one match, is suspended for a period of two years, meaning any similar offence during that period would enforce it.

The FA has also been fined €15,000 (£12,600).

The four Nations League quarter-finals will be played across two legs during the international break in March 2027.

The first legs will be played over the 25-27th March with the second legs played between 28-30th March.

The semi-finals and final will follow in June 2027 following the end of the 2026/27 domestic season.

Jurgen Klopp must be feeling confident about Germany’s chances of progressing further in the competition.

The German team haven’t been anywhere near their best so far but they’re drawn against an aging and rebuilding Beglium team in the quarter-finals.

Belgium managed to come through a pressure-filled contest against Italy in the group stage in a sign of their lasting quality but Germany will be favourites.

The Germans also have the added motivation of a possible semi-final with England to come so they should be firing on all cylinders come the quarter-finals in March.

In the third quarter-final the Netherlands will host Portugal.

Portugal have very fond memories of the Nations League having won the competition twice including the inaugural tournament.

They are also the reigning champions having beaten Spain in a penalty shootout last year.

Can the Netherlands muster up enough quality to overcome a Cristiano Ronaldo-less Portugal side and reach the final four?

Elsewhere the Nations League quarter-finals have also thrown up another World Cup rematch.

This one is from the semi-finals as Spain take on France once again.

Spain have won each of the last three knockout games against France with those coming in three different competitions.

They won 2-1 in the Euro 2024 semi-finals before a 5-4 victory in the Nations League semi-finals in 2025.

Most recently, of course, they won 2-0 in the World Cup semi-finals in a match they completely dominated.

Can France overcome them across two legs this time around?

England’s quarter-final tie against Norway will be a rematch of their meeting at this summer’s World Cup.

The Three Lions triumphed on that occasion with Jude Bellingham scoring twice to overturn Andreas Schjelderup’s opener and secure a 2-1 win after extra-time.

Norway were arguably the better team on the day though and will feel confident about challenging England over two-legs come March.

Thomas Tuchel’s men will take on Norway in the quarter-finals.

Should they progress from that tie they will face either Germany or Belgium in the semi-finals.

If they reach the final they will play one of France, Spain, Portugal or the Netherlands.

Now, a draw is made to determine the semi-final fixtures.

In the first semi-final will be the winners of quarter-final three.

They will take on the winners of quarter-final one.

In the second semi-final the winners of quarter-final four will face the winners of two.

#1031. Van Dijk uncertain on Liverpool future

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk is out of contract in the summer and told Sky Sports he has "no idea" where he will be playing next season; Watch Liverpool vs Man Utd live on Sky Sports Premier League on Sunday from 4pm; kick-off 4.30pm.

By Harriet Prior (interview) | Peter Smith (words)

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk believes he can keeping playing for "many more years" - but says he does not yet know whether that will be at Anfield next season.

The 35-year-old centre-back, who has won two Premier League titles and the Champions League during his time at Liverpool, is out of contract in the summer.

He told Sky Sports that, currently, he is uncertain on what will happen beyond this campaign.

"The main thing for me is that I feel good and I'm looking after myself and I still have many more years in my opinion," he said.

"Whatever's going to happen after this season, we'll see.

"At this moment of time, if anyone says that or put out that they know what I'm going to do next season, it's untrue because at this moment of time, speaking to you, I've got no idea either.

"But I'm relaxed with it because if you know me, I only focus on what I can control and that's at the moment the Manchester United game. Then we'll focus to the Champions League and whatever happens in the new year coming, we'll see then.

"But it's been an incredible journey, almost 10 years this summer and it's been a big part of my life and I'll forever be grateful for anything that happened over those years.

"If it's getting extended, we'll see then.

"If not, then I'm going to say goodbyes in the summer."

Asked about how emotional that exit would be, he said: "Well, yeah, probably for me the most and the family because it's been an incredible time.

"But I don't look too far in the future and that's been, in my opinion, also a little bit of a success. I won't change it now either.

Van Dijk has made a positive start to this season, partly thanks to his encouraging connection with new centre-back partner Jeremy Jacquet.

The Dutchman has been impressed by his young team-mate and says they have been working together on and off the pitch to build up their relationship and help each other perform to the highest level.

"He's been outstanding so far I must say," said Van Dijk when asked about Jacquet. "Very young but he plays like a very mature player. He's still 21, he's still going to get so much better and that's a good thing.

"Obviously, I speak to him a lot during the game but after the game and training and certain moments as well where I feel like I can help him.

"As a centre-back partnership, you have to be able to understand what your qualities and what your flaws are at times and then complement each other on those things. You only get there by playing games.

"It's been good because he's helping me, I help him and that's how it should be. I must say I'm impressed with how we started and now it's down to him to keep that level, keep that consistency, stay calm because you can easily get carried away because there's a lot of plaudits coming his way and rightly so. But I know how it can work when you have maybe one lesser game or not up to the standard that you have.

"He just has to keep going, keep staying important and be fit and then things will be working out pretty well."

#1029. How does Euro 2028 qualifying work? Confirmed pots, format, and rules for co-hosts

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland will co-host the tournament as the qualifying draw takes place in Belfast on Sunday December 6

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Co-hosted on home soil by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, the road to Euro 2028 is fast approaching as the draw for qualifying takes place in Belfast in early December.

But the four co-hosts will enter qualifying for the tournament as normal, even though there is a ‘safety net’ that can be used by two of the teams should they fail to qualify automatically.

The United Kingdom hosted some games during the Covid-delayed Euro 2020 tournament in 2021, although many matches were played with limited capacities due to Covid restrictions.

Wembley hosted the final and will do so again in 2028, with Cardiff, Glasgow, Dublin, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle also staging games during the 24-team tournament.

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, which takes place in Northern Ireland on Sunday 6 December.

Unlike previous major tournaments held in multiple countries, England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland do not qualify automatically just because they are co-hosts. Although this is a tournament for the UK and Ireland, Northern Ireland are not considered co-hosts, as they are not staging any games.

But while England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all enter qualifying as usual, there are two reserved places to be used by co-hosts if they fail to qualify automatically, either by winning their group or finishing as one of the eight-best runners-up.

The four co-hosts, as well as Northern Ireland for that matter, will all be kept apart in the qualifying draw to boost their qualification chances, so if they all go on to their win their groups then happy days – the safety net is not required.

But if disaster strikes and three or more of the co-hosts fail to qualify on merit, then there are just the two reserved places to fall back on: they will go to the two teams who have the best record in qualifying and the others will have to watch on.

The Euro 2028 qualifying draw takes place in Belfast on Sunday 6 December. Qualifying then begins in March 2027, but only for the teams not involved in the Nations League quarter-finals or Nations League play-offs who were drawn into Groups G-L. Within those groups of five, the four other teams will play against each other across March and June 2027, with everyone else then beginning their qualifying campaign from September 2027.

With the English top-flight a state of flux right now, it's not hard to yearn for years gone by.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.

The bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before. Is there a title race? Who’s going down? What is real? Does any of this mean anything? Throw in the continued abomination that is VAR and more, and it’s all just a bit bleak.

So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.

While football didn’t start in 1992, the Premier League did and by the early-to-mid 2000s, it was reaching its apex as the blood and thunder of decades prior fused with the new-found flair and panache to create a near-perfect concoction.

The current state of the English top-flight can be traced all the way back to the summer of 2003 with Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea. It was the moment the horse bolted and nothing has been the same since.

However, at the time, it was all just a little bit exciting and things really picked up 12 months later when Jose Mourinho landed in West London, rightly claiming to be the “Special One”. The reigning European Cup winner was joined by Rafael Benitez, who came to Liverpool after incredible success with Valencia.

Suddenly, Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger were no longer the only gunslingers in town. The “Big Two” quickly became the “Big Four” as Mourinho romped to the league title - breaking numerous records - and Benitez amazingly won the Champions League. Istanbul and all that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The two Iberians changed so much in the English game. From how to set up a side to how to win the title - 4-4-2 and peaking after Christmas being swapped out for 4-3-3 and rapid-fast starts.

Liverpool’s fifth European Cup was significant for numerous reasons. It was their first in 21 years but also the first final featuring an English side in the 21st century. They had beaten Chelsea to get there, starting both an incredible rivalry between the clubs and managers, and a golden age for the Premier League.

Over the next four years, all of the then-”Big Four” made finals and there were three semi-finalists in every season from 06/07 to 08/09. The peak came in 2008 when each was knocked out by another with United eventually toppling Chelsea in the first all-English final in Moscow. In one of the odder paradoxes, England failed to qualify for the European Championships that summer.

Fergie’s empire had struck back with Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney at the forefront of it. In an era of elite pairings, there was no finer. Ronaldo’s Ballon d’Or win confirmed his status as the best player in the world, and the Premier League as truly the best league.

It was also a time of far less financial disparity with the rest of Europe, Milan and Inter lifting the Champions League in 2007 and 2010 respectively. Things would soon change and not for the better.

While the big boys competed for the biggest trophies, there were plenty of brilliant stories elsewhere. Harry Redknapp’s Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008, setting the tone for Wigan five years later in epic fashion against City months on from Swansea claiming the League Cup. Only Crystal Palace's success in 2025 has been comparable since.

Throw in Big Sam’s Bolton, Blackburn, Stoke, Hull and others and it was the last definitive age of the cult teams and cult heroes, or as they’ve become better known - The Barclaysmen. With the overload of data nowadays, another Michu-like madness feels further away than ever.

Abu Dhabi’s takeover of City in 2008 is the obvious place to pinpoint the beginning of the end, but Mourinho’s first Chelsea exit a year prior and Ronaldo’s first from United a year after moved the centre of attention from England to Spain.

While European success faded - a fate-like Chelsea were the only winners from 2008 to 2019 - there were still memorable domestic moments, two of which unfortunately led to City winning their first pair of Premier League titles. Agueroooooo and Gerrard’s slip may be rendered utterly irrelevant soon but the memories won’t. It was peak Premier League.

As was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last dance in 2013 and Leicester’s miracle title win in 2016, which will never be topped as the greatest achievement in the history of English football. That it came either side of Chelsea’s crooked titles and prior to City’s dodgy dominance makes it all the more appropriate as the ending of the last great era. And that goes for both in football and the world itself.

While the on-field action of the last decade may feel fraudulent, how we now consume football is also a far cry from those halcyon Barclays days.

Streaming was not yet a thing in 2004. Sky Sports was in its pomp. Super Sunday actually lived up to its billing as appointment viewing.

Influencers and content creators had not yet taken over. Gary Neville went past his winger on the overlap rather than host it. Social media was still fun for the most part.

We had Soccer AM and Goals on Sunday, Gillette Soccer Saturday and Match of the Day at elite levels, and even room for shows like Wayne Rooney’s Street Striker and Football’s Next Star.

Nostalgia is a helluva drug, but as Independent Panels decide the fate of English football past, present and future, it’s near-impossible to dispute that, like so much of entertainment, we had it so much better before.

One day, the pendulum will hopefully swing back in our favour but, for now, a rewatch of Premier League Years on Sky may be in order.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV shows and attempting to play tennis.

#1027. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

#1025. Andriy Shevchenko slams Mykhailo Mudryk for ‘baseless slander’ after Ukraine doping claim

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Shevchenko, who is president of the Ukrainian football federation, called on Mudryk to provide evidence for his claims or retract his accusations

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ukrainian football federation president Andriy Shevchenko has issued a sharp rebuke to Mykhailo Mudryk after the Chelsea winger blamed the national team for his positive drugs test.

Mudryk tested positive for the banned substance meldonium in 2024, and was initially banned for four years by the Football Association. He successfully appealed against the length of his ban to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, and returned to football in July 2026.

Speaking in an interview with Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan at Tottenham, laid the blame on “the environment in the Ukrainian national team” for his suspension.

He said: “I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.”

He said he had only been in Ukraine with the national team, which “points to the fact it was in a national team camp”.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan forward Shevchenko, now president of the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF), called such claims “baseless slander” and said that “numerous investigations and audits” had been unable to identify how or when the meldonium entered Mudryk’s system.

He alleged that Mudryk’s camp had tried to convince a staff member at the UAF to take the blame for the 25-year-old’s positive test.

Shevchenko said: “His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

“The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work.”

Shevchenko criticised his compatriot for “baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally”, and challenged Mudryk to provide evidence for his claims, including that he had received little support from the federation during the doping case.

He added: “I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

“If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question.”

Timing is everything in football - and that goes for getting transfer moves right, too.

After seven years at Chelsea, Willian made the move across London to join Arsenal in 2020, which seemed like it should be a decent enough fit for all concerned.

But Willian has made no secret of the fact that he did not enjoy his time at the Emirates Stadium - and in hindsight, he believes he may simply have been the wrong player in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Willian told FourFourTwo: "These things happen in football. I had some personal frustrations and I couldn't perform on the pitch the way I had been performing at Chelsea.

"Arsenal were also a club that was changing a lot at that time. There were a lot of people leaving and a lot of new people coming in.

"It was a restructuring and I got caught up in the middle of it - and it's not easy.

I left a well-established club, winning almost every year, fighting for titles every year, and I joined a club that was trying to find a way to win titles again.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"So I got caught up in that situation, and that's why things didn't work out. It wasn't easy, but I really wasn't happy.

"The contract I had was actually a very big one, but it got to the point that money wasn’t enough.

"The most important thing is to be happy, to play with joy. I wasn't able to do so there, so I ended up asking to leave the club, leaving that contract behind."

After spending a year back in Brazil with Corinthians, Willian found a new home at Fulham in 2022 - and he credits Marco Silva with helping him to rediscover his spark.

He said: "When I left Brazil, my goal was to go to England, stay there, because I love the place and my agent lives there too.

"Therefore, I decided to be in London, have some meetings and see what the possibilities are. My agent said, ‘Marco Silva wants to talk to you’. We had a meeting with him, and he invited me to join training and see how I felt.

"It wasn't a trial, it was more to see if I could readjust, especially after what had happened to me at Arsenal.

"I really liked Marco’s style. I felt celebrated, and it's not flattery, but I felt that respect, that affection from everyone. I was very happy there at Fulham."

Despite Trey Nyoni's breakthrough this season, Liverpool are still light in the centre of the park

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Andoni Iraola's high press is yet to take its toll on the Liverpool squad after only 10 Premier League games, but there is every chance it will as the season wears on.

While the likes of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Alexis Mac Allister provide excellent press resistance and ball progression, for each of them to play 50-or-more games across all competitions in such a demanding system could prove untenable.

More urgent is that when the first wave of Liverpool's press is bypassed, the lack of a defensive shield leaves the backline exposed to central counter-attacks, which most notably occurred on the opening day of the new season against Newcastle.

If Liverpool are to maintain their competitive edge in the second half of the season, identifying a specialist No. 6 in the January transfer window is advisable.

According to a new data visualisation from Ballity Insight Lab analysing 68 LaLiga midfielders across the 2026/27 season, the profile Liverpool require is currently thriving in Spain. The below model plots 'duel destroyers' against 'ball-winners' seeking to find out which midfielders are good at both functions.

La Liga’s toughest midfielders? Duel Destroyer vs Ball Winner 📊 Wins it and wins duels: 🇦🇷 Guido Rodríguez, 🇪🇸 Rodri, 🇨🇴 Deossa, 🇫🇷 Camavinga, 🇪🇸 Gorrotxategi, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Bellingham, 🇩🇰 Hjulmand, 🇪🇸 Bernal, 🇫🇷 Lemar, 🇪🇸 Barrios Formula in the comments 👇 https://t.co/6rcVRo63vUNovember 16, 2026

The top-right quadrant of this scatter plot is categorised as the 'wins it and wins duels' bracket.

This zone is reserved for midfielders who consistently break up opposition play with lots of tackling and interceptions, whilst also dominating individual physical battles.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unsurprisingly, the quadrant is populated by unattainable global stars such as Real Madrid duo Eduardo Camavinga and Jude Bellingham, alongside more established anchors like Guido Rodriguez and Morten Hjulmand.

However, just beneath those household names are two statistical outliers who could be January targets for the Anfield recruitment team: Jon Gorrotxategi and Nelson Deossa.

Gorrotxategi, who like Iraola is of Basque descent and currently represents Real Sociedad, stands out as the most compelling statistical fit for Liverpool’s needs.

The Spanish midfielder is positioned near the 95th percentile in the 'duel destroyer' category while simultaneously sitting around the 88th percentile as a ball-winner.

He boasts an aggressive, front-foot defensive style that would suit the demands of Premier League football.

The data suggests Gorrotxategi could function as Liverpool's midfield backstop, sweeping up loose balls and engaging opposition ball-carriers before they can reach the Reds' defensive third.

Deossa, meanwhile, presents an intriguing, slightly more balanced alternative, which perhaps Liverpool already have covered in their midfield stable.

The Colombian midfielder ranks just below the 90th percentile for ball-winning and hovers around the 85th percentile for duels. His profile suggests he is a player who reads the game well to block passing lanes, while retaining the physical bite required to win ground duels in the middle third.

Relying on converted No. 8s, or an up-and-coming 19-year-old, to anchor a title-challenging midfield is a compromise that opponents will punish as the season deepens. Liverpool need a player capable of holding central spaces when the full-backs push high and to win second balls from clearances.

The likes of Camavinga or Hjulmand may dominate mainstream transfer gossip columns this winter, but the smart money lies in targeting the anomalies.

In going for either Gorrotxategi or Real Betis man Deossa in January, Liverpool would acquire a midfield destroyer capable of plugging the gaps and protecting the defence, ultimately freeing their more technical midfielders to focus on unlocking opposition low blocks. Neither will come cheap, though, as both players are contracted to their respective clubs until June 2030.

#1021. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

The Principality of Sealand is only half the length of a football pitch, but that hasn't stopped the tiny micronation from trying to make its grand return to international football.

In 1967, Major Roy Bates, the owner of a pirate radio station, occupied HM Fort Roughs – a fortress in the North Sea, seven miles off the Suffolk coast – and declared it a nation.

By 1975, Sealand had a flag, a constitution, an anthem and passports. Like any self-respecting country, it also needed a football team. The Sealand National Football

Association was first founded in 2003 – the entire national team was initially from Denmark, bizarrely – then revived by a Scot six years later, competing in non-FIFA matches against the likes of the Chagos Islands and Alderney. Fixtures weren't played on the offshore platform, but rather in Godalming, in Surrey. Royle Family actor Ralf Little was among those who played for the team, with former West Ham hard man Julian Dicks taking the coaching reins for a spell, before activities came to an end once more in the mid-2010s.

After a 12-year hiatus, Sealand is set to return in 2027 with both men's and women's ‘national sides', as well as a different approach.

“This team is all about spreading the message of Sealand, but we will be a proper international team ready to play other nations, both recognised and unrecognised,” director of football Ross Galbally tells FFT.

While it may appear that Sealand could struggle for a player pool (even Michael Bates, who inherited the platform from his dad, doesn't actually live there), anyone who takes up an e-citizenship of the Principality will be eligible for selection – that can be bought online for £7.99 a month, while noble titles are also available.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It costs £499.99 to become a Duke or Duchess, but just £39.99 to become a Baron or Baroness – in 2012, Ed Sheeran became Baron von Edward Sheeran of Sealand.

“Sealand's motto is ‘From the sea, freedom,'” Galbally explains. “Our team is open to anyone sharing our values. Every other country picks on citizenship and birthright, so why can't we select our team based on values?”

“THE WHOLE ADVENTURE IS ABOUT SEALAND AND ITS ETHOS, BUT ALSO THE PLAYERS' JOURNEYS”

The team's first trials will be held in early 2027, and people can apply from anywhere. There has already been interest from Argentina, the USA and Scandinavia.

“We hope Sealand will offer a second chance for players who missed out on showing their talent on the international stage,” Galbally says. “This whole adventure is about Sealand and its ethos, but also the players, their stories and their journeys.”

Sealand's managerial team is set to include coaches with experience in the EFL, as well as non-league. The executive board is a mixture of those with football backgrounds and people involved with music – a link to Sealand's pirate radio past.

The new team's inaugural game is likely to be in the UK, but matches could also take place in mainland Europe and the USA.

There are no plans to knock on FIFA or UEFA's door any time soon, and it also seems unlikely they'd meet the criteria to join CONIFA, the alternative organisation for nations, states and peoples not recognised by FIFA – current members of that organisation include Tibet, Greenland and Cornwall.

But Sealand has never been overly concerned about following the rules – from 2027, football's latest national side could be coming to a city near you.

Arsenal are in the midst of tying down key players - and not every decision they make will go down well with fans

Arsenal are set to make difficult choices behind the scenes that may not go down well with fans.

Supporter satisfaction is arguably the highest it has been since the days of the Invincibles, with manager Mikel Arteta leading Arsenal to a first Premier League title in 22 years and just a second Champions League final earlier this year.

FourFourTwo understands that with rivals undergoing uncertainty and transition, the Gunners are looking to establish a dynasty, with contract renewals on the table for several players.

While Arsenal have built a reliable core of world-class players across the pitch, however, not every one of their biggest names will be rewarded with a deal to reflect their status within the squad.

Sam Dean of The Telegraph has reported that while David Raya, Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Jurrien Timber are all out of contract within 18 months, only three – Rice, Raya and Timber – are close to signing extensions.

Of the remaining four, Merino and White perhaps do not command a place in Arteta's best XI, with the latter touted for sale over the summer before injury ruled him out of the World Cup and a departure became a little more complicated to engineer.

Club captain Odegaard has recently spoken out on his situation at London Colney, telling reporters, “I’m happy and hope I can stay there [at Arsenal] for a long time to come, but we haven’t started on that yet” – while Havertz remains one of the club's highest earners and one of Arteta's most relied-on players.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Dean followed his article with a post on X (formerly Twitter) to reaffirm that he wasn't trying to be “negative about good news” for the Gunners, noting that Gabriel, Eberechi Eze, Viktor Gyokeres, Ezri Konsa, Bruno Guimaraes and Martin Zubimendi could all be “contracted until their 30s on big wages”.

Sami Mokbel of the BBC has also broken that Piero Hincapie is in advanced negotiations over a new deal – despite only permanently joining over the summer – while his competition at left-back, Riccardo Calafiori, is in discussions to renew beyond 2029.

The North Londoners intend to address their forward line in the upcoming couple of transfer windows, having missed out on major targets over the summer in the form of Julian Alvarez, Vinicius Jr and Morgan Rogers.

Eli Junior Kroupi and Antonio Nusa remain targets for Arteta, while midfield and defence could well see churn, as major figures depart the club.

Despite recently reiterating that he will remain in N5 until the end of the season, Zubimendi has been linked with an exit, while Merino, Gyokeres, Eze, White and on-loan Ethan Nwaneri could all look for new destinations that offer improved playing time.

Arsenal travel to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

#1017. Mauricio Pochettino is Andoni Iraola’s ghost of football future and there are lessons to learn

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Iraola is on the same path once trodden by new Manchester United manager Pochettino but will hope to avoid certain pitfalls to bring glory back to Liverpool

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino begins where Jose Mourinho finished, and some would suggest that ought to have been the order of succession at Manchester United anyway. But Mourinho’s last match in charge occurred at Anfield. His United lost 3-1 as Liverpool had 36 shots. Six months later, Jurgen Klopp had another notable victory to celebrate, over Pochettino’s Tottenham in the Champions League final.

But a journey along the East Lancs Road for Pochettino’s bow with United has a pertinence for other reasons, and they stretch beyond the regular comparisons between English football’s two most storied clubs. Opposites in some respects, they are akin in others. When Pochettino looks at the home dugout on Sunday, he may see himself: not so much in the mirror as in the past.

Andoni Iraola is 44, a decade younger than Pochettino and is roughly at the point in his managerial career that the Argentinian was 10 years ago; indeed, that was when many felt United should have appointed him, in preference to the more decorated Mourinho.

Some of those similarities could be dismissed as superficial, even if they suggest Iraola was following Pochettino’s path. Each managed in LaLiga before England, then joining a South Coast club; controversially, too, given the English incumbent who had succeeded was ruthlessly sacked to make way for a man deemed more progressive.

The eventual verdict was that Southampton got an upgrade on Nigel Adkins, as Bournemouth would on Gary O’Neil. Pochettino took Saints to their joint highest finish for 24 years. Iraola recorded the best in Bournemouth’s history.

Each did so while improving players to such an extent that the established elite started buying them in bulk; indeed, Liverpool were to purchase four of Pochettino’s Saints players and, even before hiring Iraola, had taken Milos Kerkez from Bournemouth and shown an interest in Antoine Semenyo.

A reason was that they were playing a brand of football that seemed to equip them for clubs more accustomed to life nearer the top of the table, which in turn reflected the ethos of the managers. Pochettino and Iraola were not prospering by playing underdog football; a high-paced, attacking, ambitious gameplan meant they earned admirers.

Each was an evangelist for a pressing game. Each had learned from one of its great theorists, Marcelo Bielsa, even if Pochettino was more of a disciple while Iraola’s biggest managerial influence was actually Ernesto Valverde.

Parachuting either in to a superpower required a decision to prioritise potential over a proven ability to win trophies, a style of play over experience. Iraola’s only silverware as a coach has come in Cyprus. Ten years ago, and two seasons into Pochettino’s time at Tottenham, he had won nothing, and Mourinho had won everything.

A fundamental difference in thinking between Liverpool and United may have been apparent in some managerial choices. Liverpool sacked a Premier League winner, in Arne Slot, to appoint Iraola. For a time, United sought solace in silverware, in the Champions Leagues Louis van Gaal and Mourinho had claimed, but picked men who were past their best. Then they sought solace in the silverware secured in lesser leagues by Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, but picked men who became exposed in the Premier League.

Liverpool may be banking on Iraola becoming a trophy-gatherer as a consequence of combining his methods with better players and when freed from a selling club. For much of the last 13 years, United have seemed to look at the manager’s CV to provide a shortcut to success.

At times, it may have counted against Pochettino. But, as he finally takes charge of United, there is a way in which he represents a role model to Iraola. The Argentinian took the step up to bigger clubs and, without acquiring the medal collection, has offered the evidence he belongs at that level. Will Iraola, even if he does not last at Liverpool?

Because others have floundered and dropped down: to clubs with less scrutiny, or expectation about the style of play. Think of David Moyes after United or Roy Hodgson after Liverpool, or some of Pochettino’s successors at Spurs, Nuno Espirito Santo and Thomas Frank among them. In contrast, since Tottenham, Pochettino has managed Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea and remained a constant in the conversations for high-profile posts.

For some of the last decade, however, it has been unclear if his career remains on the upward trajectory it definitely was in 2016, as Iraola’s has been in 2026. Ten years ago, Pochettino seemed to have captured the Zeitgeist, perhaps in alliance with Pep Guardiola and Klopp. Now everyone presses, Pochettino is in his mid-fifties and there is a question if he is still the face of modernity.

Liverpool can note their last two Champions League-winning managers, Rafa Benitez and Klopp, were given the job at 44 and 48 respectively. United’s only unqualified success among managerial appointments since Sir Matt Busby, in Sir Alex Ferguson, was 44 when he arrived at Old Trafford.

Now Iraola is 44; a coincidence, perhaps, but the age can seem a sweet spot, offering coaches some experience while being young enough to have a connection with their players, for their ideas to have a freshness and them to exude energy. Pochettino, another smiling Spanish speaker, may glimpse a vision of what he was when he looks at Iraola. But then his test is to show he remains the man for now.

With one win in 10 Premier League games this season, is it any wonder Man United players are feeling the pressure?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there was any doubt over the scale of the task facing Mauricio Pochettino at Old Trafford, a social media exchange between one of his players and a content creator has illustrated it perfectly.

Manchester United winger Amad Diallo responded directly to an Instagram account criticising his recent display.

“Just shut your mouth, bro - you’re talking too much now,” Diallo wrote. “Go play in my place if it bothers you that much”.

While it is understandable for a young player to feel the weight of fan frustration, the optics of the situation are poor.

A Manchester United player reacting publicly to a troll on social media just days before a new manager takes charge is an indictment of the dressing room’s current mental state.

🚨📲 𝗡𝗘𝗪: Amad Diallo’s comment on a fan who criticized him: “Just shut your mouth, bro—you’re talking too much now. Go play in my place if it bothers you that much.” https://t.co/sLqd3B912HNovember 18, 2026

The incoming Pochettino will want an emotionally resilient squad, given the responsibility of representing one of the biggest clubs in world football.

This incident highlights the repair job required at Carrington, because if a highly-rated 24-year-old is spending his free time scrolling through his own mentions and biting back at criticism, it begs a much larger, more worrying question: Are all Manchester United players this hyper-aware of their online reception?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

If they are, it explains a great deal about the fragility on display during matches. A squad that lives and dies by its social media mentions is unequipped to handle the pressure cooker environment that is Old Trafford.

When things go wrong on the pitch - and they frequently do for this current iteration of Man United - players affected by outside noise are far more likely to retreat into their shells than rally together.

Pochettino’s first priority therefore cannot be tactical; it must be cultural. He has to insulate his squad from the news cycle which bounces between online praise and vitriol. The Argentine could do a lot worse than instituting a bunker mentality from day one at Old Trafford.

#1014. People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty

People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November. The analysis offers clues about why dementia rates have fallen by 13% per decade over the past 27 years in Europe and the United States2.

The researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words. The study included 219,000 people aged 50 and older who were born between 1910 and 1964, and tracked changes in their scores over three decades. These list-based tests are commonly used to screen for dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

Consistent with previous studies3, people born more recently entered old age with better memory performance compared with those born in earlier generations. A ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Memory decline also appears to have become less steep across successive generations, says study co-author Anders Fjell, a neuropsychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway.

The findings are “confirmatory” of other studies on the topic, which indicated that the rate of memory decline is slowing down but weren’t statistically significant, says Carol Brayne, an epidemiologist who studies dementia at the University of Cambridge, UK. “It is another piece of the jigsaw.”

Because many populations around the world are ageing — that is, older individuals are becoming a larger proportion of the total population — the number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide. But an individual person’s risk of dementia at any given age has dropped by two-thirds over the past 40 years in the United States4. “For those who reach 80, a smaller percentage [of people] will get dementia than before,” explains Fjell.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active

To understand what might be driving this trend, Fjell and his colleagues used longitudinal data on individuals’ cognitive performance to estimate their memory trajectories over time. The authors examined whether people born later in the twentieth century showed differences in their memory performance and their rate of memory decline compared with those born earlier.

The analysis found that with each successive birth decade, people were 64% more likely to maintain stable memory function — that is, experience little or no memory deterioration.

The authors also investigated brain imaging data from nearly 2,000 people over a median of four years. They found that a stable memory during ageing also corresponded to a decrease in shrinkage of the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory formation.

Manchester United had a long list of prospective new managers before settling on Mauricio Pochettino

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino was only hired after conversations with a leftfield former Chelsea player.

That's according to a new report, which says that Manchester United had an exhaustive list of options to manage the club, including surprise names, with different figures pulling in different directions behind the scenes.

Pochettino is taking over while the Red Devils are in the relegation zone, with the likes of Cesc Fabregas having been touted for the job – but it was another former Chelsea star who perhaps came closer to getting the nod.

In a new piece for The Athletic, Laurie Whitwell, Adam Crafton and David Ornstein have detailed the process that United took in their latest search for a new manager.

While admiration from United's Omar Berrada for Fabregas “did not develop to anything further”, it has been claimed that co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was in favour of former Blues boss Antonio Conte, whose representatives contacted the Red Devils to signal the Italian's availability.

Intriguingly, another former Stamford Bridge alumnus, Didier Deschamps, actually engaged in talks.

The 58-year-old stepped down from managing the French national team over the summer after 14 years and two World Cup finals, with the out-of-work boss a surprise candidate to take over from Carrick.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Those conversations did not go well,” the report claims, however, adding that “People at United [felt] that he was looking to gain leverage for a move to work in Saudi Arabia.”

Two Premier League managers were linked with the role in the form of Fabian Hurzeler and Unai Emery, with neither option materialising in the end after calls “via intermediaries” with the latter.

Julian Nagelsmann was an option that was nixed after United deemed it “risky” to hire someone with no experience in English football, with Stuttgart boss Sebastian Hoeness liked but also overlooked, potentially for similar reasons.

Eddie Howe was also named among the candidates, though the report states that interest in the former Newcastle and Bournemouth boss “did not progress further and he was left off the final names considered”.

United face Liverpool when Premier League action resumes this weekend.
